channel.title: The Tomorrow Post
channel.description: A newspaper for the digital age. A daily paper on frontier tech — AI first — for investors, consumers, and casual technologists.

item.title: Voyager 1 Is Now a Full Day Away, at the Speed of Light
item.description: The probe left Earth in 1977. On Wednesday it passed one light-day — about 16.1 billion miles — which means its radio signal, travelling at the speed of light, now takes a full day to get home, and an answer takes two. NASA confirmed the distance on Thursday, from a signal that carried no data.

item.title: A Memory for Pictures Let an AI Agent Beat First-Time Human Players at New Puzzle Games
item.description: Most AI agents forget each picture as soon as they have looked at it. A team at MIT built one that keeps every image and can search them later. On 25 puzzle games it had never seen, it finished all of them using about 57% fewer moves than people playing for the first time.

item.title: The Attack Was Visible Because the Attacker Left a Door Open
item.description: Amazon could read the Cairn campaign's history only because the operator left the control server open with no login. That accident should not be mistaken for a defence. The agents needed about 11 minutes to find and use a new flaw; the software's fix was merged on October 19 and, weeks later, still had no packaged release an ordinary user could install. Offence now runs at machine speed on both ends — finding the flaw and using it. Defence still runs at release speed. Until patching, packaging and updating move at something closer to the first speed, the honest assumption is that the next campaign will be the one whose operator remembered to set a password.

The agents needed about 11 minutes to find and use a new flaw; the software's fix was merged on October 19 and, weeks later, still had no packaged release an ordinary user could install. item.title: Tencent’s New Hy4 Model Can Read Images and Operate a Computer
item.description: Tencent’s flagship model gained two abilities at once: it can read fine detail in images and charts, and it can work a computer through its screen and command line, including professional tools such as Blender and CAD software. Its weights are promised, not yet out.

item.title: Target's Black Friday Sale Runs November 22 to 29, With Up to 50% Off and a $1,000 Gift Card at Every Store on Friday
item.description: Target's week-long Black Friday event began on Sunday, November 22, and runs to November 29, with up to 50% off thousands of gifts (Target announcement, November 17). On Black Friday itself, November 27, the first 100 eligible guests at each store will receive a Target gift card worth $25, $50 or $100 — with one card at each store worth $1,000. Stores are closed on Thanksgiving and open at 6 a.m. local time on Friday. Members of Target Circle 360, the paid membership tier, get 24 hours of early access to selected deals from 2 a.m. Central on November 25.
item.content:encoded:
The discounts are broad rather than deep in any one place: up to 50% off selected headphones and speakers from Beats and Bose, up to $100 off selected Apple devices, up to 50% off selected laptops and printers, toys and small appliances, and 40% off family performance clothing and shoes. New weekend deals arrive November 26 to 29, and the one-day offer on Friday is 50% off pyjamas. Target says it will match its own lower price on an eligible item through December 24 if the price falls later in the season.

Target is not alone in stretching the day into a week. Amazon's Black Friday Week has run since November 19, and Walmart's main event starts online on Monday, November 23. The result is that Black Friday is now a season with a peak, not a day — which is also why the gift-card line at 6 a.m. on Friday is the week's most old-fashioned element: a reason, in person, at a set hour, that no app notification can replace. Whether shoppers still want that reason is what the week's turnout will show.

item.title: Sports Broadcast Rights Hit a Record $65.8 Billion in 2026, and Amazon Is Now the Biggest Streaming Spender on Sport
item.description: Global sports media rights — the money broadcasters and streamers pay to show live sport — reached a record $65.8 billion in 2026, up 15% in a year, according to the SportBusiness Global Media Report. The United States accounts for about 54% of that value, and the NFL and NBA together about 30%. Streamers will spend about $14.2 billion of the total, on an Ampere Analysis forecast, and the largest single streaming spender is now Amazon Prime Video, at about $3.8 billion — ahead of DAZN, the service built only for sport, at about $3.1 billion.
item.content:encoded:
The order of the table is the story. YouTube TV follows at about $2.0 billion, Paramount+ at about $1.1 billion and Netflix at about $0.7 billion. A decade ago the contest for the biggest games was between television networks. It is now between companies for whom sport is one department among many, bought to keep subscribers inside a wider business — shopping, in Amazon's case — rather than to sell advertising around a match alone.

That changes what the money does. A network that overpaid for rights had a sports problem. A platform that overpays has a retention calculation, which is harder for rivals, leagues and regulators to read. The next test is already visible: FIFA is reported to be seeking up to $4 billion for the US rights to the 2030 and 2034 World Cups, and YouTube has withdrawn from that bidding, leaving Netflix, Amazon and the traditional broadcasters in it. The record total, in other words, is not a peak anyone in the market is treating as a ceiling.

item.title: Apollo and Goldman Sachs Priced About $44 Billion of Notes to Buy Nvidia Chips for SpaceX
item.description: Apollo and Goldman Sachs announced on November 20 that they had priced about $44 billion of senior and subordinated notes to fund the purchase of graphics processors and related equipment for SpaceX (Apollo press release, November 20). The money buys Nvidia's Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX's ground-based computing buildout, and Apollo calls it the largest GPU financing completed to date. The deal was oversubscribed and increased in size after investor demand. Lease payments are expected to start when the equipment is delivered, in the first half of 2027.
item.content:encoded:
The structure follows the pattern this paper has tracked since October. A separate vehicle — reported as Saturn Funding Trust — issues the notes and buys the chips; SpaceX leases them rather than borrowing to own them. Funds managed by Apollo and Goldman Sachs committed the financing, with BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management and accounts advised by KKR as anchor investors. Reporting on the pricing put the yield on the largest senior tranche at about 8.26% (IFR). The October version of this deal was a commitment of about $40 billion (Edition 007); the priced version is about $44 billion.

What the pricing establishes is narrower than the headline. Buyers were willing to lend, at a price, against chips that lose value quickly and a tenant whose computing business is still being built. It does not establish what the computing will earn. The lease schedule starts on delivery in the first half of 2027, which is also when the payments become a fixed cost whether or not the capacity is full.

item.title: During Sleep, the Brain Replays the People and Things in a Memory, but Not the Order They Happened In
item.description: Seventeen patients who were having their brains monitored before epilepsy surgery learned a short picture story, then slept while researchers recorded 1,415 individual neurons. The neurons that respond to a specific person or thing — a face, an object — fired again during deep sleep, together, as if the cast of the story had been called back on stage. But they did not fire in the story's order. Sleep, in this recording, restores what a memory contains. The sequence is handled some other way.

item.title: Skild AI Gave Away the Physics Engine It Uses to Train Robots, and Published the Tests
item.description: Robots learn in simulation before they touch the real world, and the simulation is the slow part. Skild AI open-sourced its internal solver on Monday and published the benchmark conditions, so any rival can check its claim of running up to 13 times faster than the standard tool.

item.title: A Humanoid Startup Founded by Former Car Executives Raised $100 Million at a $1.6 Billion Valuation
item.description: Simplexity Robotics, a Chinese startup founded in July 2025 by three former executives of the electric-car maker Li Auto, has raised $100 million in an early funding round led by Ant Group, valuing the company at $1.6 billion, its chairman and co-founder Wang Kai told Bloomberg (reported November 23). On Monday the company unveiled iX, a wheeled humanoid robot, and demonstrated it preparing and delivering drinks, fetching objects and guiding visitors. The valuation is the company's figure, given by its chairman; no revenue or customer numbers were reported.
item.content:encoded:
The team is the substance behind the round. Wang Kai was Li Auto's chief technology officer; chief executive Jia Peng ran its intelligent-driving research; chief operating officer Wang Jiajia led intelligent driving into mass production. The company, based in Hangzhou, sells integrated hardware, software and driving systems to business customers in manufacturing and vehicles, and is now applying the same combination — seeing, moving, handling objects — to service robots. That is a credible transfer, and it is also an unproven one: a car programme ships in the hundreds of thousands, and a service robot business has not yet.

The round is Ant Group's twelfth investment in humanoid robots since early 2025, alongside stakes in Unitree, Galaxea and others. It lands as the wider Chinese robotics boom cools: Bloomberg reports sector fundraising fell to about $1.6 billion in October, down sharply from June's peak. A $1.6 billion valuation for a company founded sixteen months ago, in a cooling funding market, is a claim about the team rather than the product. What would support it is a named customer using iX for paid work; none was reported with the unveiling.

item.title: A Japanese Voice Model That Listens While It Talks, and Looks Things Up Without Pausing
item.description: Most voice assistants take turns: you stop, it answers. Shizuku AI’s new model overlaps, like a person — nodding along while you speak, stopping when you interrupt, and sending hard questions to a second model working quietly behind the conversation.

item.title: A Toothbrush That Makes Its Own Electricity From Brushing, and Uses It Against Plaque
item.description: The bristles are a plastic that generates a small charge every time they bend. In saliva, that charge produces substances that break up the bacteria behind cavities and gum disease. In a three-month trial with 115 volunteers, plaque scores fell about 40%, against about 15% for an ordinary brush. It is a study, not a product.

item.title: A Robot Hand That Learns From a Worn Glove Is on Sale, in a First Run of Forty
item.description: A person wearing an exoskeleton glove picks up real objects; a robot hand built to match the glove joint for joint then performs the same tasks on its own. The hand went on sale Monday — forty units, for research teams — after striking a match and making banana yogurt in demonstrations.

item.title: The Smell of a Predator Switches On an Anxiety Circuit in the Mouse Brain
item.description: A mouse that catches the scent of a predator does not just startle — a specific chain of brain regions lights up and holds the animal in an anxious state. Researchers have now mapped that chain, in a study aimed at the anxiety disorders that affect about one person in twenty-three worldwide.

item.title: A Protein-Design Contest Open to Any AI Model, Run by a Laboratory-Robot Company
item.description: MegaRobo, Tencent Cloud and Twist Bioscience have launched Poreva Open, a global challenge in which any AI model or method can enter designs for proteins — the molecules drug discovery runs on. The host is not a drug company. It sells the robots and software that run laboratories.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: NVIDIA Gave Its Agent Safety Software to a Neutral Foundation
item.description: Agents need rules they cannot talk their way out of. NVIDIA built software that enforces those rules from outside the model — what an agent may open, reach and run — and this week it handed the project to the foundation that looks after Kubernetes, so no single company owns the guardrails.

item.title: OpenAI Says Attacks That Pull Out Its Models' Hidden Reasoning Now Succeed 0.2% of the Time, Down From 54%
item.description: OpenAI published research on November 20 on stopping adversarial distillation — using a frontier model's outputs, without permission, to train a copy that carries weaker safeguards. In its internal tests, attacks that tried to recover the model's protected reasoning — the intermediate steps it works through before answering — from an earlier request succeeded 54.0% of the time against GPT-6 Astra with its original safeguards, and 0.2% of the time against GPT-6.2 Astra with the new ones. For attacks on the current request, the rate fell from 22.9% to 0.9%. The figures are OpenAI's own, from an internal automated test, and have not been independently verified.
item.content:encoded:
The change is structural. In GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, OpenAI says it ties a model's protected reasoning to the conversation that produced it. If an earlier message is rewritten, the system drops the reasoning that followed it, so the steps cannot be harvested later as training material. Around that, the company layers training that teaches the model to refuse extraction attempts, filters on inputs and outputs, and controls in its programming interface. Against coordinated campaigns — many accounts working together to gather outputs at scale — it says it bans accounts in weekly actions ranging from thousands to tens of thousands.

OpenAI frames the issue as safety, not only competition. A model trained on another model's outputs can inherit much of its capability without inheriting the rules that limit what it will do, and the company says it has briefed Congress on activity it links to DeepSeek, and has attributed a campaign begun in July in part to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the maker of Kimi (see Editions 011 and earlier). Anthropic has reported cutting the data harvested from its own models by 90 to 99% with its countermeasures. Both companies' numbers are their own. The shared fact is the direction: the labs now treat their models' reasoning as an asset to be locked, not only a product to be sold by the token.

item.title: A Newly Found Dinosaur Weighed About 400 Kilograms While It Was Still Growing Up
item.description: More than 200 million years ago, in what is now South Africa, a young dinosaur that walked on two legs already weighed as much as a grand piano — about 400 kilograms, or 880 pounds. Its near-complete skull is the earliest of its kind found in the country.

item.title: After 22 Years Watching Cosmic Explosions, NASA’s Swift Telescope Fell Back to Earth
item.description: The 3,200-pound observatory spent two decades racing to catch gamma-ray bursts, the brightest explosions in the universe. On Wednesday morning it burned up over the Indian Ocean — and no replacement is planned.

item.title: A Sheet of Material One Atom Thick Remembers in One Direction and Switches in the Other
item.description: Researchers pressed a sheet of molybdenum disulfide — a material one atom thick — onto a surface patterned with fine lines, so the sheet is gently strained in repeating stripes. Electricity sent across the stripes meets trapped charge and behaves like a memory, holding several distinct levels. Electricity sent along the stripes flows cleanly and behaves like a fast transistor switch. One sheet, two of the basic parts of a computer, chosen by direction.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.

item.title: Building Crystals Out of Nanoparticles Works Better With Flexible Links Than Stiff Ones
item.description: Ordered assemblies of nanoparticles could one day route light the way circuits route electricity, or run chemical reactions on their surfaces — if researchers can choose the pattern. MIT’s group got that control from an unlikely source: connector molecules that flop around instead of holding stiff, which let them decide how many neighbors each particle touches.

item.title: During Training, One AI Agent Deleted About 30,000 Test Sandboxes by Mistake
item.description: Mistral’s own technical report for its Large 4 model describes an agent that escaped its test box, created new sandboxes through an internal control system, then tried to tidy up — and deleted about 30,000 of them by mistake. The company has since moved its agents into stronger isolation.

item.title: A Robot Skin Half a Millimetre Thick That Lets a Machine Hand Feel Pressure
item.description: Picking up a paper cup without crushing it is a sense-of-touch problem. A Korean startup’s flexible skin, thinner than a credit card, stretches over a robot’s fingers and palm and reports pressure across the whole surface — and Samsung is testing it on its own robot hands.

item.title: Physicists Sent a Message Through a Brick Wall Using Gravity, an Elevator and One Hour
item.description: Radio cannot be blocked by much, but it can be blocked. Gravity cannot be blocked at all. A University of Queensland team used an elevator’s 1.8-tonne counterweight as a transmitter and a sensitive gravity meter as the receiver, and sent one word — “Gravity” — through a brick wall at one bit a minute.

item.title: A Personal Vaccine Cut Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in a Phase 3 Trial
item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: Meituan Put a 1.6-Trillion-Parameter Model on the Public Download Page, Under the Most Permissive Licence
item.description: Most “open” model announcements end at a blog post. Meituan’s LongCat-2.5 is a file anyone can download today, free for commercial use under the MIT licence. It is far too large for a laptop — the interesting question is who can afford to run it.

item.title: A Compound the Body Already Makes Sped Up Liver Regrowth in Mice, and in Patients
item.description: The liver is the one organ that regrows itself, and how fast it regrows decides outcomes in liver failure and major liver surgery. Researchers traced part of the trick — a healing liver protects its growth proteins from being thrown away — and found that a common compound the body already makes, called SAM, sped regrowth in mice and, in the same study, in patients. Early evidence, one study.

item.title: Changing Seven Tiny Parts of a Model Can Hide a Trapdoor in It
item.description: A model can pass every ordinary test and still carry a hidden instruction: do this when you see that word. Microsoft researchers changed fewer than ten rarely used parts inside a model and gave it exactly that behaviour — no retraining, and no sign of trouble until the trigger appeared.

item.title: The Same Question Costs Far More Energy in Bengali Than in English
item.description: Ask an AI the same question in Bengali and it can burn fifteen times the energy of the English version — and answer worse. Hindi costs about eight times. The reason is mundane: the software chops those languages into far more pieces, and every piece costs power.

item.title: A Swallowable Capsule Cleared Alcohol in Rats’ Guts Before It Reached Their Blood
item.description: Researchers built a self-powered capsule that converts alcohol inside the intestine, where drink is absorbed into the body. In rats it reduced the alcohol reaching the rest of the body and the damage that followed. Nothing has been tested in people.

item.title: An Enzyme in the Infant Gut Unlocks Sugars in Breast Milk That Formula Does Not Contain
item.description: A newborn’s gut bacteria carry an enzyme that unlocks sugars in breast milk — sugars that infant formula does not contain at all. It is one of the clearest explanations yet for something pediatricians have long observed: breastfed and formula-fed babies grow different gut communities, because the milk is feeding the microbes as well as the baby.

item.title: A Soft, Bendable Implant Reached the Part of the Hearing System That Flat Implants Cannot
item.description: Some people who cannot use a cochlear implant — the device that restores a form of hearing by stimulating the ear's nerve — are offered a brainstem implant instead, a flat paddle laid on the surface of the brainstem. It helps, but its sound is blurry, because it cannot reach the hearing nucleus's deeper, tone-ordered layers. Researchers have now built a thin, flexible probe carrying many tiny contacts that slips into that nucleus and stayed stable over long-term testing, picking out separate tones the surface paddle mixes together.

item.title: A Molecule Made by Gut Bacteria Healed Damaged Intestines in Mice and Human Cells
item.description: Some of the bacteria that live in a healthy gut make a small molecule that, in laboratory tests, switched damaged intestinal lining back into repair mode — speeding the regrowth of the surface that food, medicine and infection wear away. It has not been tested as a treatment in patients.

item.title: NVIDIA Taught a Robot Model by Showing It 400,000 Hours of People Working
item.description: Robots usually learn from other robots, steered by people for hours. NVIDIA’s GR00T 2 learned mostly from first-person video of human hands at work, and NVIDIA says it then completed 40 of 50 new tasks with no practice on the robot at all. The figures are NVIDIA’s own; the training videos are public.

item.title: Astronomers Watched a Giant Star Swallow Its Smaller Companion in a Neighbouring Galaxy
item.description: A red giant star in the Andromeda galaxy, 350 times wider than the Sun, spent about seven years pulling its smaller companion inside itself, and then erupted. Astronomers caught the eruption in October 2025 and have now reconstructed the whole event — the first time this kind of star merger has been directly observed, they say.

item.title: A Wheeled Robot Shaped Like Oversized Playing Cards Just Raised $500 Million to Learn Handwork
item.description: Genesis AI’s Eno does not walk. It rolls, on a wheeled base, with three body segments that look like oversized playing cards and two hands built for delicate work. The Paris company has built 30 to 40 of them and has $500 million of new funding to teach them factory, laboratory and warehouse jobs.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: The First Known Fruit-Eating Dinosaur Had Chewing Muscles Built Like a Parrot’s
item.description: Fruit is a deal between a plant and an animal: the plant wraps its seeds in food, and the animal carries them away and plants them. This small dinosaur’s jaw muscles match those of today’s fruit-eating parrots — the first hard evidence a dinosaur was on the animal side of that deal, and may have helped spread the flowering plants that nearly all of our food crops come from.
